mri-scan-what-to-expect.name: MRI scan: what to expect and what it shows
mri-scan-what-to-expect.summary: An MRI scan uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not X-rays, to take detailed pictures. This guide covers noise, safety checks, contrast and results.
keyPoints: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to take detailed pictures, and it does not use X-rays.
The scanner is loud, so earplugs or headphones are provided, and staff can talk to the person through an intercom.
A safety questionnaire is completed first because some implanted devices can stop a scan from going ahead.
Results are not usually given on the day: a radiologist reports the images to the doctor who requested the scan.

body.heading: What is an MRI scan?
body.body:
Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to take very detailed pictures from almost every angle. It does not use X-rays or other ionising radiation. Coils placed around the part of the body being studied help to send and receive the radio waves and improve the quality of the pictures. The person operating the scanner watches from another room.

Scan length depends on the area examined, and NHS trust leaflets quote different times, from about 10 minutes to about 90 minutes. One trust says the total time in the department is likely to be about an hour.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body:
Staff settle the person on a couch that slides into the scanner. An intercom lets the person talk to the radiographer, and a call button is provided. The person is asked to keep still, because movement can blur the pictures.

Some scans include an injection of contrast, a dye that helps to produce a more detailed picture and improves the accuracy of the scan. MedlinePlus says contrast is usually given through a vein, and that the most common agent contains gadolinium. It adds that allergic reactions to this substance rarely occur. MedlinePlus also says gadolinium can be harmful for people with kidney problems who need dialysis, so kidney health is a standard question before a contrast scan.

body.heading: Why is the scanner so loud, and what if it feels enclosed?
body.body: The scanner makes loud beeping or hammering noises, so earplugs or headphones are provided and some departments play music. MedlinePlus notes that some people feel claustrophobic, which means anxious in enclosed spaces. Trust leaflets say some people find the scan difficult for this reason. They list options such as visiting the department beforehand, using a wider scanner, techniques that staff can use during the scan, or a mild sedative prescribed by a GP. A person who has a sedative needs someone to take them home afterwards.

body.heading: Is an MRI scan safe, and why is metal a concern?
body.body:
Before the scan each person completes a safety questionnaire. York Hospitals says there are no known risks from an MRI scan when a person meets the safety standards. The magnet can make pacemakers, artificial limbs and other implanted devices that contain metal malfunction or heat up, according to MedlinePlus. Loose metal objects can be pulled toward the magnet and cause injury. For that reason removable metal, such as jewellery and watches, comes off before the scan.

Some implants, such as certain brain aneurysm clips or programmable shunts, may mean a scan cannot be done. Implants made of non-magnetic material are usually labelled MR safe or MR conditional, and some pacemakers can be scanned under strict conditions, according to a safety review. Trust leaflets ask people to tell the imaging staff about any implants. MedlinePlus says tattoo dyes can irritate the skin or eyes, and medication patches can cause a skin burn.

body.heading: Do I need to prepare?
body.body: Usually no preparation is needed, and people can typically eat and drink as normal. Some scans of the abdomen or pelvis may need fasting for a few hours, and bowel-relaxing medicine is sometimes given.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: Results are not usually given on the day of the scan. A radiologist, a doctor who specialises in reading scans, studies the images and writes a report for the doctor who requested the scan. That doctor then discusses the findings with the person. The main extra risks come from the injection, as a small chance of a reaction to the contrast, and rare discomfort or tissue damage if the cannula, the small tube in the vein, leaks. Trouble breathing or swelling of the face after an injection would need a 999 call.

ct-scan-what-to-expect.name: CT scan: what happens, contrast and radiation
ct-scan-what-to-expect.summary: A CT scan uses X-rays and a computer to build slice pictures of the body. This guide covers preparation, contrast dye, radiation and when results arrive.
keyPoints: A CT scanner rotates an X-ray source around the body, and a computer builds cross-sectional slices that can be stacked into a three-dimensional picture.
CT uses more radiation than a standard X-ray, the amount is kept as low as possible, and the risk from a single scan is small.
Some scans use an injected iodine-based dye called contrast, which can cause a warm flush and a metallic taste that usually pass quickly.
A radiologist reviews the images and sends a report to the doctor who requested the scan, who then discusses it with the person.

body.heading: What is a CT scan?
body.body: CT stands for computed tomography. A CT scanner rotates an X-ray source around the body while the person lies on a bed that moves through a ring shaped like a doughnut. Detectors on the opposite side pick up the X-rays, and a computer turns each rotation into a thin cross-sectional slice. The slices can be stacked to make a three-dimensional image. The NHS lists CT scans among the tests that use X-rays to give more detailed images than a standard X-ray.

body.heading: How do people prepare for a CT scan?
body.body: Instructions differ between hospitals, and the appointment letter has the local details. One trust asks for no food for two hours and about half a litre of water beforehand, while another asks for no solid food for four hours and says drinks are fine. Some scans of the abdomen or pelvis need a larger amount of fluid or a drink containing contrast beforehand. Some people have a blood test first, mainly to check how well the kidneys are working. Metal items such as zips, jewellery and clips may need to come off, and a gown may be provided. Staff ask about allergies, especially to iodine or to earlier contrast dye, and about medicines the person takes.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: The person lies on a flat, motorised table that slides into the scanner. They are asked to keep very still and may be asked to hold their breath for a few seconds. Sources give different lengths for the scan itself, from a few minutes to around 20 minutes, and a visit can last an hour or two. MedlinePlus says the scan is painless but can be uncomfortable because the person has to stay still. Most people can go home or return to normal activities straight away.

body.heading: What is the contrast dye?
body.body:
Contrast is a substance that makes blood vessels, organs or other tissues easier to see. Depending on the area, it may be given by mouth, through a vein, or by enema. The type given through a vein usually contains iodine, and trust leaflets state that it is not radioactive. It goes in through a small tube, called a cannula, in the arm or hand. It can cause a warm flush, a metallic taste or a feeling of needing to pass urine, and these usually pass quickly.

Serious allergic reactions are rare, and milder reactions such as a rash, itching or nausea are possible. Rarely the dye leaks into the tissue around the vein and causes swelling or discomfort. Effects on the kidneys are uncommon and occur mainly in people who already have kidney problems, so staff check kidney function and sometimes suggest extra fluids. Some trusts ask people to wait for a short time after an injection so staff can check for a delayed reaction. Difficulty breathing or swelling of the face after an injection is an emergency, and a 999 call is the route.

body.heading: How much radiation does a CT scan use?
body.body: CT uses ionising radiation, and the dose is higher than for a standard X-ray, although staff keep it as low as possible. MedlinePlus says having many X-rays or CT scans over time may raise the risk of cancer, but the risk from any one scan is small. Children are more sensitive to radiation, and scanner settings for children are adjusted to lower the dose. Trust leaflets say people who might be pregnant should check with the department before the scan. The NHS describes X-ray tests as safe, with a very small cancer risk linked to having many of them. GOV.UK safety advice describes the risks from properly justified imaging as far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated, and the added chance of cancer as very small and appearing years or decades later. It lists CT among the examinations that carry a low risk even though they involve more images or higher doses. Trust leaflets add that the benefit of a scan usually outweighs the small risk.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: A radiologist reviews the images and sends a report to the doctor who asked for the scan. That doctor then discusses the results with the person. Timing varies by hospital, and leaflets quote from about one or two weeks to about four weeks. Results are not given on the day.

x-ray-what-to-expect.name: X-ray: what to expect, safety and results
x-ray-what-to-expect.summary: An X-ray uses a small beam of radiation to picture bones, lungs and other parts. This guide covers the test, radiation risk, pregnancy and results.
keyPoints: An X-ray can produce images of many parts of the body, and the NHS lists fractures, teeth, lungs and the digestive system among them.
The NHS describes X-rays as safe, with serious complications rare and a very small cancer risk linked to having lots of them.
Trust leaflets say X-rays in pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage or birth defects, and that those of the abdomen and pelvis are usually avoided.
Results may be given on the same day or at an appointment some weeks later, depending on the type of X-ray.

body.heading: What is an X-ray used for?
body.body: An X-ray uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation to make an image of the inside of the body. According to the NHS, X-rays can produce images of many parts of the body, including bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system. They are used, for example, to check for broken bones after an accident. A trust leaflet says that specially trained staff check each request first, to confirm the test is the right one for the person and their condition.

body.heading: What happens during an X-ray?
body.body: The health professional who takes X-rays in hospital is called a radiographer. The radiographer positions the person sitting, lying or standing, depending on the part of the body. The X-ray itself takes only a few minutes, according to the NHS. The NHS says people are asked to remove metal items such as jewellery and zips. Some types need fasting for several hours beforehand.

body.heading: Which other tests use X-rays?
body.body: The NHS lists several related tests, including angiography, which checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood. It also lists DEXA scans, which measure bone density, and CT scans, which give more detailed images. Studies of the digestive system use a barium drink or enema, a liquid that shows up on X-ray. After a dye or barium test, the NHS says people may be asked to wait for up to 30 minutes so staff can check for a reaction.

body.heading: How much radiation is involved?
body.body: The NHS says X-rays are safe and serious complications are rare. It adds that there is a very small risk of cancer linked to having lots of X-rays. Trust leaflets say staff keep doses as low as possible and that a test goes ahead only when its benefit outweighs the small risk. GOV.UK safety advice says that when imaging is properly justified and optimised, the risks from X-ray examinations are far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated. It describes the added chance of cancer as very small, and says any effect would appear years or decades later. The same advice says children have a higher lifetime risk from X-rays than adults, and that risk is lower for older patients because cancers take a long time to develop. These leaflets give their own figures for the risk, and the figures differ between leaflets, so the radiographer or the doctor who requested the test is the person to ask.

body.heading: Are X-rays safe in pregnancy?
body.body: Trusts ask anyone who might be pregnant to tell the team before an X-ray. A Leicester hospitals leaflet says X-rays during pregnancy do not increase the risk of miscarriage, birth defects or developmental problems. The main concern it names is a very small increase in the chance that the baby develops cancer in childhood. X-rays of the abdomen and pelvis are usually avoided in pregnancy. X-rays of parts of the body well away from the abdomen, such as arms and legs, and dental X-rays, do not give any increased risk to an unborn baby, according to the same leaflet. When an urgent test is needed, a radiologist and the doctor who asked for it decide together whether it should go ahead.

body.heading: How and when do results come back?
body.body: A reporting radiographer or a radiologist, a doctor who specialises in imaging, reviews the X-ray. The report goes to the team that requested the test. The NHS says results may come on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later, and that a clinician should explain them. The wait varies with how urgent the X-ray is.

NHS trust leaflet (yourhealth.leicestershospitals): leic xray preg

ultrasound-scan-what-to-expect.name: Ultrasound scan: what happens and is it safe
ultrasound-scan-what-to-expect.summary: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves, not radiation, to make live pictures. This guide covers the gel, the full bladder, internal scans and results.
keyPoints: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves rather than radiation, and NHS leaflets describe it as low risk.
A water-based gel goes on the skin, and a small probe is moved over the area being scanned.
Scans of the pelvis, kidneys or bladder usually need a full bladder, and the appointment letter explains this.
Some people have an internal (transvaginal) scan to give more information.

body.heading: What is an ultrasound scan?
body.body: An ultrasound scan uses high-frequency sound waves to make a picture of the inside of the body. The sound waves bounce off different parts of the body, and the echoes are picked up by a probe and turned into a moving image. It does not use radiation or X-rays. NHS pages say it helps doctors to examine symptoms, to see inside the body during other procedures, and to monitor pregnancy. It can also help to guide a biopsy or the draining of fluid. Ultrasound is generally less effective than CT or MRI at imaging through bone or air.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: The person lies on a couch, and the room may be dimmed so the screen is easier to see. Gel is put on the skin over the area, and the sonographer or radiologist moves a small probe over it while watching the pictures. The gel is water-based and washes off easily, and trust leaflets say it will not stain clothing. Trust leaflets say the scan takes about 20 minutes in many cases, though the length depends on the area examined. Afterwards the gel is wiped off, the person can get dressed, and they can usually leave straight away.

body.heading: Why do some scans need a full bladder?
body.body: For scans of the pelvis, kidneys or bladder, people are usually asked to arrive with a full bladder. One trust explains that a full bladder pushes the womb into a position that is easier to scan. Leaflets ask people not to pass urine until after the scan, and say that anyone who becomes uncomfortably full during the scan can tell the staff and may be able to leave the room to empty their bladder before it is finished. Scans of some organs, such as the liver, may need no food for several hours beforehand. The appointment letter gives the exact instructions for each type of scan.

body.heading: What are the different kinds of ultrasound scan?
body.body: The usual scan is external, with the probe on the skin. Some people have a transvaginal (internal) scan to provide more information about the pelvis. For this scan the probe is disinfected, covered with a protective sheath and lubricated with gel. People usually need to empty their bladder first for an internal scan. A bladder scan is a quick scan that measures the volume of urine in the bladder, and it is often used to check how well the bladder empties. Ultrasound can also be used to look at blood flow and at whether blood vessels are narrowed or blocked.

body.heading: Is an ultrasound scan safe?
body.body: NHS leaflets describe ultrasound as safe and low risk, and one says it does not use radiation. The NHS pregnancy pages describe scans as painless and with no known side effects. A possible minor problem is skin irritation or infection from the gel, which wiping the gel off thoroughly after the scan helps to prevent, according to one leaflet. People with a latex allergy are asked to tell the department beforehand so latex-free products can be used.

body.heading: When are the results shared?
body.body: A sonographer or radiologist interprets the pictures. The report goes to the doctor or team who requested the scan. One trust says the findings are combined with other clinical information and discussed with the person as part of their treatment plan. How soon a report is ready depends on the local service, and one trust says most reports are ready 24 hours after the scan.

references.title: NHS trust leaflet (nth): nth pelv us

ecg-what-it-records-and-shows.name: ECG: what it records and what it can show
ecg-what-it-records-and-shows.summary: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity through patches on the skin. This guide covers the test, longer recordings, what it shows and its limits.
keyPoints: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, including its rate and rhythm.
A standard ECG is quick and painless, and patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest.
A standard tracing can show an abnormal rhythm only if it is happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.
An ECG can help to show whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one, but other tests may be needed to confirm a diagnosis.

body.heading: What does an ECG record?
body.body: An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the electrical activity of the heart. The British Heart Foundation describes it as a simple test that records the heart's rhythm, its rate and its electrical activity. Each heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the machine picks these signals up through sensors on the skin. The result is a graph of the signals.

body.heading: What happens during a standard ECG?
body.body: Sticky patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest and connected to the machine. A standard 12-lead test uses about ten electrodes to produce twelve views of the heart's signals. NHS 111 Wales describes the test as usually quick and painless. A Whittington Health page says it takes about ten minutes and is not uncomfortable. A trust leaflet says the skin may be lightly abraded or shaved so the patches stick, and that creams or oils should not be used on the day. The same leaflet stresses staying relaxed and still, because muscle movement can disturb the recording. Trust pages differ on preparation: one says none is needed, and another says people can eat and drink as normal.

body.heading: What can an ECG show?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an ECG can help doctors to tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past. Trust factsheets list abnormal heart rhythms, called arrhythmias, coronary heart disease, heart attacks and cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle, among the conditions it can help to diagnose or monitor. The tracing can also show features that suggest a person may be at risk of an abnormal rhythm, according to the BHF.

body.heading: What are the limits of a standard ECG?
body.body: A standard ECG captures only what happens while it is recording. It can show an abnormal rhythm only if the rhythm is happening at that time. A Sussex factsheet notes that the test has limitations, so further tests may be needed to confirm a diagnosis. That is why longer recordings or other heart tests are sometimes arranged.

body.heading: What are longer and exercise ECGs?
body.body: An ambulatory ECG, sometimes called Holter monitoring, records the heart's electrical activity continuously while the person goes about daily life. The BHF says it records for 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer. It is used for symptoms that come and go, such as palpitations, and it can help to diagnose conditions such as atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm. One NHS summary says the length of wear is decided by the consultant or GP and can be between 24 hours and seven days. An exercise ECG monitors the heart while the person exercises and the heart is working harder. The BHF describes it as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, and says it shows whether the heart muscle is getting enough blood through the coronary arteries during activity. Doctors often use it to look into symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, dizziness and breathlessness. It is also used after procedures such as angioplasty, and to help set exercise levels for cardiac rehabilitation. The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gets harder over time, and can stop at any point if they feel unwell.

body.heading: How do the results reach the person?
body.body: The report goes to the doctor who requested the ECG. That doctor then contacts the person to discuss the result. For the exercise test, the BHF says the results are sent to the person's doctor, and that the wait can range from a few days to a few weeks. Anyone with chest pain that is severe, spreading or accompanied by breathlessness should call 999 and not wait for a test appointment.

echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows.name: Echocardiogram: types, what happens and results
echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows.summary: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to picture the heart. This guide explains the standard, stress and throat versions and what each involves.
keyPoints: The most common type is a transthoracic echocardiogram, in which a probe is placed over the chest.
A stress echocardiogram is done during exercise or after a medicine that has a similar effect on the heart.
A transoesophageal echocardiogram passes a probe down the throat and gives more detailed pictures than the standard test.
Most people need no preparation for a standard echocardiogram, but may need to avoid eating for several hours before the throat version.

body.heading: What is an echocardiogram?
body.body: An echocardiogram is a scan that uses ultrasound, high-frequency sound waves, to produce moving pictures of the heart. An ultrasound probe covered in water-based gel is placed on the chest in the standard test. The sources describe this test as causing little or no discomfort.

body.heading: What are the types of echocardiogram?
body.body: The most common type is the transthoracic echocardiogram, in which the probe is placed over the chest. A transoesophageal echocardiogram uses a probe that passes down the throat and gives more detailed pictures of the heart than the standard test. Doctors may use it when the standard test has not shown enough detail. A stress echocardiogram is a transthoracic scan done during exercise on a treadmill or exercise bike, or after a medicine that has a similar effect on the heart. A contrast echocardiogram uses a harmless substance injected into the bloodstream to produce a clearer image. A stress echocardiogram may be recommended if a heart problem is triggered by physical activity.

body.heading: What happens in the throat version?
body.body: For the transoesophageal test, the back of the throat is numbed with an anaesthetic spray. People can ask for a sedative, a medicine that leaves them very drowsy but not asleep. Avoiding food for several hours beforehand may be needed for this version. Afterwards the throat may be sore, and this should pass within one or two days.

body.heading: What can an echocardiogram show?
body.body: The NHS says the transoesophageal version can show problems with the heart valves, blood clots within the heart, problems with the aorta, and areas of heart muscle that are not working properly after a heart attack. The more detailed pictures from this version can help to plan heart surgery. A stress echocardiogram uses pictures taken while the heart is under stress to make a diagnosis.

body.heading: What does it check, and how long does it take?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an echocardiogram uses ultrasound to show the size of the heart, how well it pumps and whether the valves are working. It describes the test as an important investigation for anyone with suspected heart failure, heart valve problems or cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle. The test is painless and does not use radiation. Sources give different times for the scan, and the NHS and the BHF give figures from about 20 minutes to about 45 minutes depending on the type.

body.heading: When are the results given?
body.body: Results are usually not given on the day, although a doctor may sometimes be able to talk through the findings the same day. Most people wait a few weeks, according to the leaflets retrieved. The sonographer, the specialist who performs the scan, writes a report that goes to the referring doctor, who discusses it with the person. Some leaflets say that a person who has heard nothing after a few weeks should contact the doctor who referred them.

body.heading: Is any preparation needed?
body.body: For a standard echocardiogram people usually need to do nothing to prepare. The exception is the throat version, which may require avoiding eating for several hours.

colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens.name: Colonoscopy: preparation and what happens
colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens.summary: A colonoscopy uses a thin camera to look inside the large bowel. This guide covers bowel preparation, sedation, risks and when results arrive.
keyPoints: A colonoscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the bowel to look for the cause of symptoms, to screen for bowel cancer, or to follow up earlier problems.
The bowel must be empty for a clear view, so a laxative preparation is taken beforehand and often causes frequent diarrhoea.
Polyps, which are growths on the bowel lining, can be removed during the test and examined under a microscope.
Perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, is the main serious risk and is uncommon, with higher risk when polyps are removed.

body.heading: Why is a colonoscopy done?
body.body: The NHS says a colonoscopy is often done to find the cause of bowel symptoms. Other reasons include looking for early signs of bowel cancer in people at high risk, and checking after earlier treatment for bowel cancer. People who have had polyps removed before, or who have a family history of bowel cancer, may also be referred.

body.heading: How is the bowel prepared?
body.body: For a clear view, the bowel needs to be empty. Trusts generally prescribe a laxative solution, often a powder mixed with water, to empty the bowel. One trust describes the preparation as taking laxatives, cutting down on fibre, and stopping all food in the last few hours beforehand. Leaflets warn of frequent diarrhoea, cramping and nausea, and advise staying near a toilet. One trust notes that the laxative can cause dehydration, light-headedness, low blood pressure or kidney problems. Preparation details differ between trusts, and the hospital sends its own instructions.

body.heading: What happens during the procedure?
body.body: A nurse sees the person first to discuss their medical history, carry out simple checks and explain what will happen. A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the anus and around the large bowel. Air is pumped in to open the bowel, which can cause bloating or cramps. The NHS says a colonoscopy can be uncomfortable but should not be painful. The procedure itself takes about 30 to 45 minutes, and a person may be at the hospital for about two hours in total. A leaflet says some people have sedation, some breathe a pain-relieving gas called Entonox, and some have no pain relief. Sedation is given through a small needle in the back of the hand.

body.heading: What are polyps and biopsies?
body.body: Polyps are growths on the bowel lining, and they are usually not cancer. It is not possible to tell by looking whether a polyp contains cancer cells, so polyps are removed and examined under a microscope. Staff can also take small tissue samples, called biopsies, which is painless. Afterwards the person is usually told whether any polyps were removed or samples taken.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body: The NHS describes colonoscopy as a common and straightforward procedure. The main risks are a tear in the bowel wall, called perforation, and bleeding. Trust leaflets give perforation figures that differ, and one says it happens to about one person in 1,000 nationally. The risk rises when polyps are removed, especially large or complex ones. Sometimes a hole can be closed with clips during the procedure. It is common to pass a small amount of blood from the anus after a biopsy or polyp removal. Colonoscopy is very accurate, but occasionally a problem, including rarely a cancer, can be missed. Severe belly pain, heavy bleeding or a fever after the test needs urgent help: NHS 111 or the hospital unit, and 999 if it is severe.

body.heading: When do the results come?
body.body: A letter or call with the results usually comes two to three weeks after a colonoscopy. A normal result means no polyps or cancer were found in the bowel. If a biopsy was taken, the biopsy results can take up to two weeks.

references.title: NHS trust leaflet (cht): cht colo prep

gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp.name: Gastroscopy: what happens and what to expect
gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp.summary: A gastroscopy uses a thin camera to look at the gullet and stomach. This guide covers fasting, throat spray or sedation, risks and results.
keyPoints: A gastroscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the mouth and down to the stomach.
The stomach needs to be empty, and trusts ask for a fast of several hours beforehand.
People can have a throat spray and stay awake, or sedation that leaves them relaxed and drowsy.
Serious complications are rare, but a person who has severe stomach pain or vomits blood afterwards should call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What is a gastroscopy?
body.body: A gastroscopy is a test in which a thin, flexible tube with a small camera goes into the mouth, or sometimes the nose, and down into the stomach. The doctor or nurse watches the lining of the gullet, stomach and the first part of the small bowel on a screen. Tiny tissue samples, called biopsies, may be taken, and this is painless.

body.heading: How do people prepare?
body.body: The stomach must be empty, so trusts ask people to stop eating for about six hours beforehand. Clear fluids are usually allowed in small sips until about two hours before the test. One trust explains that an empty stomach matters because sedation can allow food to enter the lungs and cause an infection.

body.heading: Throat spray or sedation: what is the difference?
body.body: People usually choose between a throat spray and sedation. The throat spray is a local anaesthetic that numbs the back of the throat, and the person stays awake while a nurse talks them through the test. For sedation, a small tube called a cannula is placed in a vein, usually in the back of the hand. The medicine makes the person relaxed and drowsy, but not fully asleep, and they may not remember the test afterwards.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body: Air is passed in to inflate the stomach, which can cause bloating and burping. The test usually takes between 5 and 20 minutes. Common effects include a sore throat and stomach discomfort, which pass within a few hours.

body.heading: What happens afterwards?
body.body: After a throat spray, people can usually leave straight away, though the throat stays numb for up to an hour and eating and drinking wait until the feeling returns. After sedation, the person rests in a recovery area for a couple of hours. They need to bring someone with them and go home by car or taxi, because the sedative can stay in the body for 24 hours. Leaflets advise avoiding driving, alcohol and signing important documents for 24 hours.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body: Serious complications are rare, and one leaflet says they occur in fewer than 1 in 500 tests. Possible problems include a tear in the gut wall that may need surgery, bleeding, and an allergic reaction to the sedation or throat spray. Sedation can affect breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, which is why staff monitor them. Rare complications include damage to loose teeth, crowns or bridgework. A leaflet says to call 999 or go to A&E if stomach pain gets worse or if the person vomits blood.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: People are told the main findings before they leave and get a written summary to take home. Biopsy results from the laboratory are not available on the day. They go to the GP or specialist and usually take two to three weeks.

spirometry-lung-function-test-explained.name: Spirometry: the lung function test explained
spirometry-lung-function-test-explained.summary: Spirometry measures how much air the lungs hold and how fast it can be blown out. This guide covers the test, preparation and what results are compared with.
keyPoints: In spirometry the person breathes through a mouthpiece, with a nose clip, into a machine that measures airflow.
Each blow is repeated at least three times, with rests in between.
Results are compared with values predicted for someone of the same height, age and sex.
The test may be repeated after a reliever inhaler to see whether the airways open up.

body.heading: What is spirometry?
body.body: Spirometry is the most common lung function test. It measures how much air the lungs can hold and how quickly air can be blown out. Lung function tests give an indication of the capacity of the lungs and how clear the airways are.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body: The person wears a nose clip so air goes through the mouth, and breathes through a mouthpiece into the lung function machine. They breathe normally, take a deep breath in, and then blow out as hard and fast as possible. Each blow is repeated at least three times, with enough rest in between. The test usually takes about 15 minutes.

body.heading: How do people prepare?
body.body: One NHS practice suggests avoiding vigorous exercise for 30 minutes before the test. The same guidance suggests wearing loose clothing, removing loose-fitting dentures and chewing gum, and emptying the bladder. It also asks people to tell staff about a recent chest infection that needed antibiotics or steroids, or a heart attack in the last three months. Practices differ, so the appointment letter has the exact instructions.

body.heading: What is the reliever step?
body.body: The test is often repeated after a reliever inhaler to check whether it helps the airways. The person takes the test, uses the inhaler, waits a short time and repeats the test. A clear improvement suggests that the airways respond to the medicine, which supports a diagnosis of asthma.

body.heading: What do the results show?
body.body: Results are compared with predicted values for someone of the same height, age and sex. The laboratory report shows the reference values used for the comparison. In obstructive conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways narrow, making it harder for air to flow out of the lungs. Restrictive conditions are different, because they decrease the amount of air the lungs can hold. A respiratory doctor reviews the results and, if needed, arranges a follow-up appointment to explain them. If no follow-up is needed, the results go directly to the GP.

body.heading: Are there any risks?
body.body: NHS leaflets say there are no direct risks from lung function tests. The effort can be tiring, and people are given time to recover between tests. Some people feel dizzy or faint, and coughing is common.

dxa-bone-density-scan-explained.name: DXA bone density scan: what it shows
dxa-bone-density-scan-explained.summary: A DXA scan measures bone density at the hip and spine using very low-dose X-rays. This guide covers who is offered one and what the T-score does and does not decide.
keyPoints: A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a padded table while a scanning arm passes over the hips and spine.
The radiation dose is low, and a Royal Marsden leaflet describes the added risk as extremely small.
The T-score compares bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
The decision to offer a medicine rests on the overall chance of breaking a bone in the next ten years, not on the scan result alone.

body.heading: What is a DXA scan?
body.body: DXA, also written DEXA, stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan that measures bone density. The scan is used to help diagnose osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker. The NHS lists DEXA among the tests that use X-rays.

body.heading: Who is offered one?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales says a scan may be offered to people over 50 who are at risk of osteoporosis. It also says people under 50 may be offered one if they have other risk factors, such as smoking or a previous broken bone. A doctor usually makes the referral. Results are combined with a fracture risk assessment rather than used alone.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: The person lies on their back on a padded table. A scanning arm passes over the body, usually the hips and spine, and the images go to a computer. The scan is painless and takes between about 5 and 15 minutes, depending on the sources and the body part scanned.

body.heading: How much radiation is involved?
body.body: The dose is low. A Royal Marsden leaflet describes the added risk as extremely small and says there are no side effects of bone density scanning.

body.heading: What do the T-score and Z-score mean?
body.body: The T-score compares a person's bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex. Scores fall into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis, and the laboratory report shows the bands used. Osteoporosis is diagnosed using the lowest T-score across the lumbar spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip. The Z-score compares a person with others of the same age, and it is used mainly for premenopausal women, men under 50 and children.

body.heading: Does the result decide treatment?
body.body: A T-score does not decide treatment alone. The Royal Osteoporosis Society says the decision to offer a medicine is based on the overall chance of breaking a bone in the next ten years, rather than only on bone density.

breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec.name: Breast screening: who is invited and what happens
breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec.summary: NHS breast screening uses mammograms to look for cancers too small to see or feel. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment, results and harms.
keyPoints: The NHS offers breast screening from age 50 up to the 71st birthday, with invitations every three years.
A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast, with each breast pressed between two plates.
Screening aims to find breast cancers at an early stage, when they are too small to see or feel, and it does not prevent breast cancer.
Screening can miss a cancer and can raise false alarms, and some people are diagnosed with a cancer that would never have caused harm.

body.heading: Who is invited for breast screening?
body.body: The NHS says screening is offered from age 50 up to the 71st birthday. The first invitation comes between the ages of 50 and 53, and further invitations follow every three years until the 71st birthday. Anyone registered with a GP as female is invited automatically. People over 71 are not invited automatically but can ask for screening every three years. For trans and non-binary people, invitations depend on the sex registered with the GP, and the NHS says people who have taken feminising hormones for more than two years can have screening.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast. Each breast is pressed between two plates, which is likely to be uncomfortable, and some people find it painful, but it is over quickly. Sources describe an appointment as taking roughly 20 to 30 minutes, and one unit suggests allowing up to an hour.

body.heading: How and when are the results given?
body.body: Results usually come within two weeks of the appointment and are also sent to the GP. A normal result means another invitation in three years. If the mammogram looks abnormal, the person is called back for more tests, such as a breast ultrasound scan or a biopsy. The NHS says about four in every 100 women are asked to come back, and of these, one will be found to have cancer.

body.heading: What are the benefits?
body.body: Screening aims to find breast cancers at an early stage, when they are too small to see or feel. It does not prevent breast cancer.

body.heading: What are the harms and limits?
body.body: Mammograms use a very low dose of X-rays, and the benefits are judged to greatly outweigh that risk. Screening does not always find a cancer that is there, so some people with breast cancer are missed. A mammogram can flag something in a person who does not have cancer, which can cause anxiety and lead to more tests such as a biopsy. Some people who are screened are diagnosed and treated for a breast cancer that would never have been found or caused them harm.

body.heading: What if there is a lump between screens?
body.body: Screening is not a substitute for noticing changes, and a new lump, change in shape or nipple discharge needs a GP appointment, with no wait for the next invitation.

cervical-screening-what-to-expect.name: Cervical screening: what happens and results
cervical-screening-what-to-expect.summary: Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment and what each result means.
keyPoints: The NHS in England invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening.
The sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus that can lead to cell changes.
A negative HPV result means the risk of cervical cancer is very low, and the next routine test is usually in five years.
Most people who have a colposcopy do not have cervical cancer.

body.heading: Who is invited and how often?
body.body: The NHS invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 in England, and the first invitation arrives a few months before the 25th birthday. People registered as female with a GP are invited automatically. Trans men and non-binary people who are registered differently may need to ask through their GP or a sexual health or transgender clinic. Routine screening is every five years. Since 1 July 2025, people aged 25 to 49 with a negative HPV test have moved from a three-year to a five-year interval. Invitations usually stop at 65, and a person is invited again only if a recent test was abnormal.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: Most screening takes place at a GP surgery, and a person can ask for a female nurse or doctor. The person undresses from the waist down behind a screen and lies back on a bed. The clinician gently puts a smooth, tube-shaped tool called a speculum into the vagina, and a soft brush collects a sample of cells from the cervix. The test itself takes under five minutes, and the whole appointment is about ten minutes. People can ask for a smaller speculum, ask to stop at any time, or ask to insert the speculum themselves. Light spotting for a few hours afterwards is normal.

body.heading: Why is the sample tested for HPV?
body.body: Current NHS practice tests the sample for high-risk HPV first. The NHS England guide says high-risk HPV can cause abnormal cell changes that may lead to cervical cancer. If HPV is found, the laboratory then looks more closely at the cells for changes.

body.heading: What do the results mean?
body.body: If no HPV is found, the NHS says the risk of cervical cancer is very low, and routine screening is usually five years later. If HPV is found but the cells are normal, the person is usually retested in about 12 months. If HPV continues after two years, an invitation for a colposcopy follows. If HPV is found with abnormal cells, the person is referred for a colposcopy. An unclear sample means a repeat test, which does not mean anything is wrong. Results usually arrive by letter, and one source gives two weeks, sometimes longer.

body.heading: What is a colposcopy?
body.body: A colposcopy is a closer look at the cervix, done in a hospital or clinic. The NHS says most people who have one do not have cervical cancer. Biopsy results grade the cell changes: low-grade changes usually need no immediate treatment, and high-grade changes are offered treatment to remove the cells.

body.heading: Bleeding or symptoms between screens
body.body: Unusual vaginal bleeding, such as between periods or after sex, needs a GP appointment, because screening is not meant for symptoms.
